Figure 2:Shared environments and data composition of OpenFlyV2-130K.(A) Thirteen environments supporting both navigation and VQA:
four AirSim environments, two Unreal Engine city environments,
and seven 3DGS reconstructions of real campuses and post-disaster ruins.
(B) Distribution of 72,352 navigation trajectories across the
environments.
(C) Distribution of 60,006 VQA pairs across color recognition,
object description, distance estimation, spatial relationship
reasoning, and visual grounding.

Figure 3:Aerial vision-language understanding and spatial reasoning with OpenFlyV2.(A) Distance estimation for the building marked in green: 179 m
compared with a reference distance of approximately 180 m.
(B) Description of the building within the yellow box.
(C) Relative-distance reasoning identifies the red-box building
as closer to the camera than the blue-box building.
(D) Localization of a language-described target. The predicted
bounding box (dashed orange) and reference box (solid cyan)
have an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.753.

Figure 4:Quantitative evaluation of aerial understanding and navigation.(A) Comparison with general-purpose vision-language models on color
recognition, description generation, visual grounding, distance estimation,
and spatial relationship reasoning. Visual grounding is reported as accuracy
at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (Acc@0.5), and distance estimation is shown as
relative error.
(B) Navigation performance in seen and unseen simulated environments,
measured by success rate (SR), oracle success rate (OSR), success
weighted by path length (SPL), and navigation error (NE). The
navigation baselines were trained on our aerial navigation dataset
and evaluated on the same 800 seen and 300 unseen episodes as
OpenFlyV2. Success requires an explicit stop within 25 m of the goal.
Blue and orange bars in (B) indicate seen and unseen environments,
respectively. Arrows indicate the direction of better performance.

Figure 5:Onboard aerial vision-language navigation.Three physical flight trials performed by OpenFlyV2 on a DJI M30T,
with all navigation inference executed on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.

Figure 6:Architecture of OpenFlyV2.(A)A shared vision-language backbone encodes the current image, instruction, and memory tokens to condition action generation.(B)Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM) compresses historical action segments and their visual anchors into compact event-level tokens.(C)The Motion-Structured Prior (MSP) selects and adjusts a data-derived motion prototype to construct the action source distribution. The action expert transforms a sample from this distribution into the final action chunk through conditional flow matching.
